title: Compromise Infrastructure: Server
summary: This sub-technique covers taking over third-party servers, rather than buying or renting them, and using them to stage, launch, and sustain an operation. Under the parent technique, the compromised asset here is a server with an established role, and that role shapes how the intrusion is used: a web server may host a watering hole that serves exploits to selected visitors, while a mail server may be used to send phishing messages that pass the recipient's checks because the sending host has real history. Control traffic may also be relayed through the host so that defenders see a normal partner or vendor address. The distinguishing telemetry is server-side and role-specific: web content and file modification times, new scheduled tasks or services, mail queue and relay anomalies, authentication from unexpected locations for service accounts, and outbound connections that do not match the server's function. Legitimate maintenance is separated by change tickets, deployment windows, file integrity baselines, and whether the same edits appear only on internet-facing hosts.

beginner.definition: A server is a computer that provides a service, such as a website or email. This sub-technique is about an attacker taking control of a server that belongs to another organisation. The parent technique covers compromising other people's infrastructure. Here the asset is a third-party server with a real role.
beginner.whyItMatters: A compromised web server can quietly serve harmful content to the people who trust it. A compromised mail server can send convincing phishing messages. The original owner may keep operating normally, so the abuse continues for months. Victims then blame a company that is itself a victim.
howItWorks: The attacker finds a weakness in an internet-facing server, such as an old content system or weak password.
They gain access and quietly modify website files or mail settings the server already uses.
The server then delivers harmful content or messages to visitors and recipients.
They add hidden accounts or scheduled tasks so their access survives cleanup attempts.
The server may also relay control traffic, so defenders see a trusted partner address.
When noticed, they remove their tools and attempt to enter through another provider or host.
beginner.example: Think of a pharmacy that dispenses prescriptions. Someone swaps one jar on the shelf for a lookalike. Customers keep coming to the trusted counter and receive the wrong medicine. The pharmacist is honest and busy, and the shelf still looks properly stocked.
takeaways: File integrity monitoring on web and mail servers reveals content that changed without a ticket.
Servers should have documented roles, so unexpected outbound traffic stands out.
If your server is abused, you are a victim too, but you must still warn affected users.

objectives: Explain how this sub-technique differs from the parent Compromise Infrastructure technique.
Describe how web and mail server roles are abused for delivery and control.
Identify server-side artefacts such as changed files, new tasks, and queue anomalies.
Distinguish authorised server maintenance from attacker modification.
Describe the containment steps for a server used to attack other organisations.
